content: Write a detailed explanation, about 900 words, of how a write-ahead log works in a relational database. Cover commit ordering, crash recovery, checkpointing, group commit, and the trade-offs against shadow paging. Use full paragraphs of prose, no bullet lists, do not call any tool, and do not ask me any questions.

A write-ahead log, usually called a WAL, is a sequential record of changes that a relational database writes before it writes the corresponding modified data pages to their permanent locations. Its central rule is simple: the log record describing a change must reach durable storage before the changed database page is allowed to reach durable storage. This ordering allows the database to recover from a crash by examining the log and determining which changes must be redone, which transactions must be undone, and which operations were safely committed.

When a transaction modifies a row, the database usually does not immediately overwrite the table page on disk. Instead, it changes a copy of that page in memory, often held in a buffer pool, and creates a log record describing the modification. The record may contain the affected page identifier, the transaction identifier, the changed values, and sometimes a physical description of the old and new bytes. More sophisticated systems may use physiological logging, which combines logical information about a database object with physical information about a page. Each log record receives a monotonically increasing log sequence number, or LSN. The LSN provides an ordering over changes and allows the database to determine whether a page already includes a particular log record.

The “write-ahead” requirement applies at two related levels. Before a dirty data page is flushed from memory to disk, all log records needed to describe the changes on that page must already be durable. In addition, when a transaction commits, its commit record must be forced to durable storage before the database acknowledges success to the client. This means that a client receiving a successful commit response can rely on the transaction surviving a process failure or machine crash, assuming the storage system honors the database’s durability requests. The database may write data pages later, but it has already preserved enough information in the log to reconstruct the committed changes.

Commit ordering is therefore governed by the order in which commit-related log records become durable, not merely by the order in which application code calls commit. Suppose transaction A performs its final update before transaction B, but B’s commit record reaches stable storage first. After a crash, B may be considered committed while A is not, depending on the database’s transaction protocol and visibility rules. Systems generally assign log sequence numbers in a coherent order and ensure that the required log records are flushed in a way consistent with their commit semantics. If transactions depend on one another, additional mechanisms may be required to preserve dependency ordering. For example, a transaction cannot safely commit based on data written by another transaction unless the relevant earlier transaction’s effects are durable or otherwise recoverable according to the database’s rules.

A commit does not necessarily mean that every modified table page has already been written to its final disk location. WAL permits a database to use a “steal” policy, in which dirty pages belonging to uncommitted transactions may be written out to free memory or manage cache pressure. Because those pages can contain uncommitted changes, recovery must be able to undo them after a crash. WAL also permits a “no-force” policy, in which pages modified by a committed transaction do not have to be forced to disk at commit time. The log contains enough information to redo those changes later. The combination of steal and no-force policies is efficient, but it makes recovery more important and usually requires both undo and redo processing.

Crash recovery typically begins by identifying the relevant portion of the log, often using metadata recorded in checkpoints. The recovery algorithm examines log records and reconstructs the state of transactions and pages at the time of failure. In a redo phase, it reapplies changes that should exist in the database but may not have reached disk before the crash. Redo must be idempotent or guarded by page LSNs so that applying the same log record more than once does not corrupt the database. When a log record is replayed, the recovery process can compare its LSN with the page’s stored LSN. If the page already reflects that record, the operation is skipped; otherwise, it is applied.

The undo phase handles transactions that had not committed when the crash occurred. Their changes may have reached disk because of the steal policy, so recovery reverses them using information in the log. Many systems write compensation log records while undoing. These records document the rollback itself and ensure that recovery remains restartable if another crash occurs during recovery. A transaction is treated as committed only if its commit record is present durably in the log. If its updates appear in the data files but its commit record does not, recovery removes them or otherwise restores the database to a state in which the incomplete transaction has no effect.

Checkpointing limits the amount of the log that must be analyzed after a crash. Without checkpoints, recovery might need to scan the entire history of the database. During a checkpoint, the database records information such as the active transactions, dirty pages, and a position in the log. It may also flush some or all dirty pages, depending on the checkpoint type. A fuzzy checkpoint can continue serving transactions while recording a consistent recovery boundary; it does not require stopping all activity. After a crash, recovery can usually begin near the checkpoint rather than at the beginning of the log, though it may still need to inspect earlier records for pages or transactions whose state crosses the checkpoint boundary. Checkpoints create I/O work and can cause latency if implemented poorly, so databases often spread checkpoint flushing over time.

Group commit improves the efficiency of commit processing by allowing several transactions to share one log flush. If many transactions commit close together, the database can append all their commit records to the in-memory log buffer and issue one durable write or flush operation. Once that operation completes, it can acknowledge all of those commits. This reduces the cost of storage synchronization, which is often much more expensive than copying data into memory. Group commit may increase the latency of an individual transaction slightly because it waits briefly for other commits to join the group, but it substantially improves throughput. Modern databases may combine group commit with parallel log writers, batching, and specialized durable storage interfaces.

Shadow paging provides a different approach to crash consistency. Instead of recording changes in a sequential log and eventually updating pages in place, a shadow-paging system writes modified pages to new locations. The old page structure remains unchanged until the transaction is ready to commit, at which point a root pointer or mapping structure is atomically switched to refer to the new version. A crash before that pointer switch leaves the old version valid; a crash after it leaves the new version valid. This can simplify certain recovery operations because there may be no need to replay or undo an arbitrary sequence of changes.

However, shadow paging has trade-offs. Updating many pages can create substantial page-copying and fragmentation overhead, and maintaining or atomically replacing the page map can be expensive. It can also complicate sharing, fine-grained concurrency, long transactions, and efficient space reclamation. WAL generally performs better for workloads with many small updates because sequential log writes are efficient and data pages can be flushed asynchronously. Its cost is implementation complexity: recovery must carefully coordinate redo, undo, checkpoints, transaction state, page LSNs, and durable commit ordering. Shadow paging favors simpler version-based recovery, while WAL favors high throughput, flexible buffer management, and efficient incremental updates. Most mature relational databases choose WAL because its sequential logging model scales well across large databases and diverse transactional workloads.
